title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite, eternal, and full of stars, why isn't the whole sky as bright as the Sun?
summary: A simple question about the night sky turns out to unravel assumptions about infinity, cosmic time, and the size of the universe itself.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and the sky is mostly black, dotted with points of light. This seems obvious enough that it's easy to miss how strange it actually is. If the universe is infinite in extent, eternal in age, and roughly uniformly filled with stars, then every single line of sight from Earth should eventually terminate on the surface of some star. The whole sky should blaze as brightly as the Sun's surface, day and night. It doesn't. Why not?

The Naive Argument

Imagine standing in an infinitely large forest with trees scattered evenly throughout. No matter which direction you look, your line of sight eventually hits a tree trunk—the forest looks like a solid wall of wood if it goes on forever. Stars work the same way in this thought experiment. A star twice as far away looks a quarter as bright (inverse square law), but there are also four times as many stars at that distance in a thin spherical shell around you. The dimming and the crowding exactly cancel. Every shell of space, near or far, contributes the same amount of light. Add up infinitely many shells and you get infinite brightness. This is Olbers' Paradox, named for the 19th-century astronomer who popularized it, though Kepler and others had wrestled with it earlier.

The Resolution Isn't What You'd Guess

Many people's first instinct is dust: surely interstellar dust blocks the distant light. It doesn't work—dust would absorb starlight and heat up until it re-radiated exactly as much energy as it absorbed, becoming as bright as the stars themselves. The real resolution is that the universe is not infinitely old. It's about 13.8 billion years old, so light from anything farther than about 13.8 billion light-years hasn't had time to reach us yet. Our sky is dark because we're only seeing a finite bubble of stars, not because the universe lacks them.

A second, subtler factor compounds this: the universe is expanding, so light from very distant, very old sources gets redshifted—stretched into infrared and beyond—and loses energy along the way. Even within the visible bubble, the earliest light (the cosmic microwave background) has been stretched from blazing plasma-temperature radiation down to a feeble microwave glow just a few degrees above absolute zero. The sky isn't dark because there's no light out there; it's dark because most of that light has been finite in reach and stretched into wavelengths our eyes can't see.

Why a Simple Question Became Cosmology

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable is how much it reveals from so little. Just by reasoning carefully about a dark sky, you can conclude the universe must have a finite age, or a finite reach of light, or both—centuries before anyone had direct evidence of the Big Bang. It's a rare case where pure logic about an everyday observation forces a conclusion about the origin of everything. Edgar Allan Poe, of all people, sketched a version of this argument in his 1848 prose poem Eureka, reasoning that the finite speed of light must leave gaps in a young universe's visible sky.

What's Still Unsettled

The standard resolution is solid, but it opens onto genuinely open territory: what lies beyond our observable bubble is unknown and perhaps unknowable in principle, since light from there hasn't reached us and, if the universe keeps expanding, some of it never will. We can't rule out that space extends infinitely with infinitely more stars we'll simply never see. The paradox that once seemed like an argument for a finite universe now reads more precisely as an argument for a finite observable universe—a much weaker, and much stranger, claim.

perspectives.title: Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: The dark sky is direct observational evidence for a finite age of the universe, correlating with independent measurements like the cosmic microwave background and stellar redshifts.

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: Cosmic expansion redshifts ancient light out of visibility, converting what would be blinding radiation into the faint microwave background we detect today.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox predates modern cosmology by centuries, showing how a simple observational puzzle can force theoretical conclusions long before technology can confirm them.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' Paradox is a model case of inference to the best explanation: ruling out candidate explanations, like dust, by checking whether they are physically self-consistent.
